newsitem.title: RUSSIA: World Bank sees $3 billion a year for Russia.
newsitem.headline: World Bank sees $3 billion a year for Russia.

text.p: The World Bank could lend Russia $3 billion a year over the next two years, mainly in projects dealing with the painful social consequences of economic reform, the head of the World Bank said on Monday.
World Bank President James Wolfensohn said the international development bank's initial aim was to complete its existing 28 projects in Russia, for which $4 billion remained to be spent.
But the bank was also studying further projects worth $6 billion over two years, with $2 billion a year going on social programmes, he told a news conference.
He was speaking after a five-day visit in which he met President Boris Yeltsin and the two senior economic policy cabinet ministers, Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov.
"Those loans will be directed to issues of pensions, back salaries, social programmes," he said.
Some of these projects would be involved with Russia's crisis-hit coal industry.
The rest of the $6 billion would be put into project loans in areas such as municipal reform, housing, agriculture, health and education.
The new programme is designed to start immediately, with some money paid out by autumn, when financial pressures traditionally build up in Russia.
Wolfensohn said he hoped to reach agreement this year on $3 billion, with a significant transfer of funds by December.
The bank wants its money to finance productive projects, not just to plug gaps in the Russian budget, he said.

"It's in everybody's interest to move from budget lending to lending for investment and self-sustaining economic activity... Nobody wants to borrow foreign currency for domestic budget purposes," he said.

"Our objective is to move from that sort of lending as soon as possible into lending which is related to structural reform and investment programmes and economic reforms, so that this country, which is a powerful country, can self-finance its budget."
But in the short term it might be necessary to use World Bank funds for urgent social needs, he said.

The World Bank is not putting pressure on Russia to restructure its natural monopolies, such as Gazprom GAZP.RTS, the world's biggest gas producer, and national power group Unified Energy System (UES) EESR.RTS, which is Russia's biggest company, he said.
But the government is keen to make them more efficient, and money would be available in the planned programmes to help with the dislocation of restructuring the industrial giants, he said.
This could involve funding social programmes arising from restructuring large employers, money for retraining, and new investment in the industries.

Another area where the bank could help is relocating thousands of employees from companies undergoing restructuring which are situated in inhospitable parts of Russia, where the companies are the only reason to live, such as Norilsk Nickel in the Far North, he said.
An initial project involving 50,000 people could be drawn up soon, he said.

The World Bank is also speeding up disbursements of its agreed loans to Russia, following a critical review of its portfolio early last year which found that too little money was reaching its target too slowly.
Disbursements are now running at $70 million a month against $25 million a year ago, and the bank is aiming for more than $1 billion a year, Wolfensohn said.
--Jonathan Lynn, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
